summary: The reader is built to laugh at Pigsy, cheer the monkey's mischief and triumphs, chafe at the monk's gullibility, and marvel at a crowded heaven.

need-to-breathe.why: Nothing is built to affect the reader's breath.

hungry.why: Pigsy's feasts and the peaches of immortality are described with relish enough to stir a reader's appetite a little.

full.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

thirsty.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

gassy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

need-to-poop.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

need-to-pee.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

sleepy.why: The novel does not aim to lull.

nauseous.why: Nothing is built to sicken the reader.

urge-to-sneeze.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

urge-to-cough.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

dizzy.why: Nothing is built to produce vertigo.

fatigued.why: The reader is not made to feel bodily exertion.

pain.why: The fillet spell and the beatings are comic rather than built to make the reader wince.

disgusted.why: Demons steaming monks, spider webs from navels, and Pigsy's filth are built for a shudder of comic disgust.

itchy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

tickled.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

over-stimulated.why: Nothing is built to overwhelm the senses.

too-hot-too-cold.why: The Flaming Mountain is described, not built to make the reader sweat.

afraid.why: The demons' lairs and plans to eat Sanzang give a child reader frights, lightened by comedy.

anxious.why: The reader worries briefly each time Sanzang is captured, knowing Wukong will come.

panic.why: Nothing is built to produce panic in the reader.

sensory-pleasures.why: Heavenly banquets and immortal wine are described for the reader's vicarious enjoyment.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: The inset poems describing mountains, palaces, and battles are built for the reader's pleasure in verse.

piquancy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

fun-excitement.why: Wukong's transformations, cloud-somersaults, and staff fights are built as pure adventure fun, episode after episode.

orgasm.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

love-romantic.why: The Queen of Women's proposal is comic; nothing is built to make the reader feel love.

love-family.why: The master-disciple bond and Princess Iron Fan's grief for Red Boy give faint family feeling.

grief.why: Wukong's tears at banishment give a brief pang; the novel does not dwell on loss.

missing-someone.why: Wukong gazing east toward his master is built for a moment of felt separation.

aroused-sexually.why: Pigsy's lust is a joke; nothing is built to arouse the reader.

liking-as-a-friend.why: The reader is built to love the bickering foursome and to feel their bond when Wukong is banished and recalled.

empathy.why: The reader feels Wukong's exasperation and Pigsy's cravings from inside; the novel is generous with its rogues' feelings.

compassion.why: The reader pities the villagers in demon-ridden kingdoms and the children of Bhikshu, and the monkey crushed under the mountain.

grateful.why: Nothing is built to make the reader grateful.

pleasure-from-helping.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

trustful-distrustful.why: The reader sees the demon behind each kindly old woman before Sanzang does, a dramatic irony the episodes repeat.

depressed.why: Nothing is built to lower the reader's mood.

angry.why: Sanzang's unjust fillet spells are built to anger the reader on Wukong's behalf, mildly.

envious.why: Nothing is built to produce envy.

jealous-romantic-sexual.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

jealous-friendship.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

hatred.why: The demons are foils, not built to be hated.

contempt.why: The pompous Jade Emperor, the greedy abbot, and the bribe-seeking disciples at Vulture Peak are built for the reader's scorn.

resentment.why: The reader shares Wukong's grievance at heaven's slights and at his master's injustice.

proud.why: Nothing is built to make the reader proud.

amused.why: Pigsy's gluttony and lust, Wukong's taunts, the pregnancies from the river, and the deflating of gods make the novel built for laughter.

sense-of-belonging.why: The reader joins the pilgrim band in spirit but is not recruited to a cause.

lonely.why: Wukong's five hundred years under the mountain give a moment of felt isolation.

judgy-moral-sense.why: The reader is invited to judge heaven's pettiness, Sanzang's blind mercy, and the demons' crimes, and to weigh Wukong's punishments.

admiration.why: Wukong's seventy-two transformations, his staff, and his wits are built to make the reader admire him without reserve.

embarrassed.why: Pigsy strung up by the Bodhisattvas and the monks' pregnancies are built for secondhand embarrassment.

shame.why: Nothing is built to shame the reader.

guilt.why: Nothing is built to make the reader guilty.

sad.why: Sanzang's tears and Wukong's banishment give brief sadness in a comic novel.

happy.why: The pilgrims' feasts and the final enlightenment are built to leave the reader content.

joyful-euphoric.why: Wukong's havoc in heaven and each demon's defeat are built as exultant triumphs.

effort.why: A hundred chapters of repeating ordeals ask real persistence of a reader.

focused-in-flow.why: The best episodes, the havoc in heaven and the Flaming Mountain, are built to absorb the reader completely.

bored.why: The ordeals repeat a pattern eighty-one times, and the middle chapters can bore, a risk of the design.

impatient.why: The reader is made to chafe at Sanzang's dithering and Pigsy's delays.

curious.why: The reader wants to know what each demon really is and whose escaped pet it will turn out to be.

surprised.why: The blank scriptures and the disguised demons' unmaskings are built to startle, within a familiar pattern.

awe.why: Buddha's palm, the heavenly court, and Vulture Peak are built to produce wonder at the cosmos's scale.

skeptical-doubtful.why: The reader is made to doubt each kindly stranger and each too-good monastery before the characters do.

feeling-of-knowing.why: The reader half-recognizes demons from their earlier appearances in heaven, a designed game of identification.

confused.why: The crowds of gods, bodhisattvas, and demons can confuse a first-time reader, though not by design.

frustrated.why: Sanzang's gullibility and his banishment of Wukong are built to frustrate the reader on the monkey's behalf.

uncertain-certain.why: The reader is rarely in doubt that the pilgrims will prevail.

understanding.why: The allegory of the mind-monkey disciplined is built to dawn on the reader by the end.

inspired.why: The blank scriptures are built as a koan that may give the reader a flash of insight.

satisfied.why: Each ordeal closes with the demon beaten, and the arrival at Vulture Peak and the pilgrims' Buddhahood close the whole.

foreboding.why: Each dark mountain promises a demon, a dread the reader learns to expect with relish.

nostalgia.why: Wukong's lost paradise at Flower-Fruit Mountain gives the reader a faint backward longing.

anticipation-suspense.why: Each capture of Sanzang sets a clock the reader watches until Wukong arrives.

hope.why: The reader hopes with the pilgrims for the scriptures and for Wukong's freedom from the fillet.

schadenfreude.why: Pigsy's humiliations and the gods' deflation are built to be enjoyed.

elevation.why: Guanyin's mercy and the pilgrims' final enlightenment lift the reader a little.

infatuation.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

rage.why: Wukong's havoc in heaven carries the reader along in glee rather than rage.
